concepts.name: Ecosystem Definition
concepts.description: Learner should understand what constitutes an ecosystem, including biotic and abiotic components.
concepts.evidence: All the interacting organisms in an area, together with the non-living constituents of the environment, form an ecosystem.

concepts.name: Producers
concepts.description: Learner should know which organisms produce their own food and the term used for them.
concepts.evidence: All green plants and certain blue-green algae, which can produce their own food by photosynthesis, are called producers.

concepts.name: Consumers
concepts.description: Learner should recognize organisms that obtain food from producers and their categories.
concepts.evidence: Organisms that depend on the producers, directly or indirectly, for sustenance are called consumers; they can be classed as herbivores, carnivores, omnivores and parasites.

concepts.name: Decomposers
concepts.description: Learner should understand the role of microorganisms in breaking down dead material.
concepts.evidence: Microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi break down the dead remains and waste products of organisms; they are called decomposers.

concepts.name: Trophic Levels
concepts.description: Learner should identify the hierarchical levels in a food chain.
concepts.evidence: Each step or level of the food chain forms a trophic level.

concepts.name: Ten Percent Law
concepts.description: Learner should know the approximate energy transfer efficiency between trophic levels.
concepts.evidence: On average, about ten percent of the organic matter of each trophic level reaches the next level of consumers; this is known as the ten percent law.

concepts.name: Food Web
concepts.description: Learner should understand that feeding relationships form an interconnected network.
concepts.evidence: In nature, feeding relationships are interconnected rather than isolated, forming a network of food chains called a food web.

concepts.name: Biological Magnification
concepts.description: Learner should grasp how non‑degradable chemicals accumulate up the food chain.
concepts.evidence: This increase in the concentration of harmful chemicals at successive trophic levels is called biological magnification.

concepts.name: Ozone Layer
concepts.description: Learner should know the protective role of stratospheric ozone against UV radiation.
concepts.evidence: Ozone at higher levels is a product of UV radiation acting on oxygen.

concepts.name: Biodegradable Waste
concepts.description: Learner should identify materials that can be broken down by biological processes.
concepts.evidence: Substances that are broken down by biological processes, such as the action of bacteria or other saprophytes, are said to be biodegradable; examples include vegetable peels, paper and cotton.

concepts.name: Non‑Biodegradable Waste
concepts.description: Learner should recognize materials that persist in the environment and do not decompose biologically.
concepts.evidence: Substances that are not broken down in this manner, such as plastics, glass and many synthetic chemicals, are said to be non-biodegradable; they may be inert and simply persist in the environment for a long time, or they may harm the various members of the ecosystem.
